Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Vignette:
Marcus is a 55-year-old bomb disposal technician, a role that for decades had demanded precision, calm, and a near-superhuman tolerance for the unpredictable. His trauma, however, came not from a wire or a detonator, but from the sky. Two years ago, during a drive through a midwestern town, he was caught in a sudden, violent tornado. He had pulled the car under an overpass, but the wind tore the vehicle sideways, and debris smashed the windows. He remembers the roar—a deep, deafening freight-train sound—and the screaming of a woman trapped in a car nearby, her cries swallowed by the wind. What struck him most was the utter unpredictability: the sky had been grey but not apocalyptic, and within minutes the world inverted. He tried to anchor himself, to think strategically as his training dictated, but there was nothing to disarm. The tornado lifted the other car and hurled it into a field. The woman survived, but Marcus has never been able to hold the entire event in his mind. When he tries to recall what happened next—how long he lay there, how he got out—the memory splinters. He pushes it away before it fully forms, as if his brain refuses to run the whole tape. What remains is a searing, wordless rage: at the storm, at himself, at the sheer indifference of the event. When the memory surfaces, even in fragments, his fists clench and his jaw locks; he has to leave the room to keep from shouting or breaking something.

In the months since, Marcus’s life has narrowed. He used to enjoy quiet evenings with his wife, Carol, but now he dreads any situation that might bring unpredictability. He has started avoiding family gatherings where conversations might turn argumentative—shouting, even in jest, makes him jump. A car backfiring on the street can send him into a full-body flinch, his heart hammering before his mind registers the sound as harmless. He has caught himself reacting to the garage door closing too fast, his body coiled for danger before he can think. At work, he once froze for a full second when a colleague slammed a metal locker; the false alarm felt real, and he had to excuse himself. He is terrified that one day his body will betray him at the wrong moment—that he will react to an imaginary threat and make a fatal error with a live device. To keep the fear at bay, he keeps his mind occupied constantly. He listens to dense podcasts during his commute, plays puzzle games on his phone during breaks, and volunteers for the most technical, detail-heavy assignments because they leave no room for intrusive images. But the distraction drains him, and at home he turns to food—he eats mechanically, often past fullness, as though filling himself physically might quiet the internal vigilance.

Carol has noticed the changes. He used to be engaged, teasing her about her gardening, but now he retreats to the garage or turns the television up loud. She has tried to talk to him about the tornado, but he cuts her off, saying he doesn’t want to “go there.” The overeating has added twenty pounds, and his primary care doctor has flagged his blood pressure. Marcus knows the avoidance is costing him, but he is certain that if he stops distracting himself, the missing pieces of that day will flood back and overwhelm him. What finally brought him to seek help was a flashback three weeks ago. He was in the grocery store when a child shouted near the cereal aisle. For an instant, he was back under the overpass—the roar, the screaming, the helpless rage. He dropped his basket and stood frozen, panting, until a store employee asked if he was okay. He felt humiliated and terrified of what might happen next time. He told Carol he needed to “fix this,” and she found him a therapist who specializes in trauma. Marcus is afraid of what he will find if he lets himself remember fully, but he is also tired—tired of eating his fear, tired of jumping at shadows, tired of the rage that lives just beneath his skin. He hopes someone can help him put the pieces together without breaking him further.
